mitm.title: Opt-in phone/computer decryption
mitm.intro: Install a root certificate generated on this machine, point that device's HTTPS proxy at the address below, and you'll see that device's own plaintext traffic — the same usage model as Surge, Burp, or mitmproxy. A device that hasn't installed the cert fails to connect outright; it never falls back to plaintext silently.
mitm.disabledBody: Add this to config.yaml (or flip enabled to true) and restart the agent.
mitm.proxyAddressHint: Put this in the device's Wi-Fi / HTTPS proxy settings
mitm.fingerprintHint: Check this against what the device shows after installing
mitm.downloadHint: On an iPhone, iPad, or Mac, use the one on the right — the install prompt shows a real name and description instead of a stray filename. Android and Windows should use the one on the left.
mitm.platformTitle: What installing the cert doesn't do by itself

android.name: Android
android.caveat: Settings → Install a certificate → CA certificate is all it takes, but Android 7+ trusts only system-preinstalled roots by default for apps targeting API 24+. A user-installed CA is ignored by anything that pins its own certs (banking apps, some social apps) — only the system browser and similarly unpinned apps get decrypted.

ios.name: iOS / iPadOS
ios.caveat: After installing the profile, go to Settings → General → About → Certificate Trust Settings and switch on full trust for it by hand — Apple requires this extra step for every user-added root, and the profile can't skip it for you.

macos.name: macOS
macos.caveat: Double-clicking the cert opens Keychain Access; you still have to manually set its trust to "Always Trust" — the default "Use System Defaults" does nothing.

windows.name: Windows
windows.caveat: In the certificate import wizard, make sure to place it under "Trusted Root Certification Authorities" — dropping it into "Personal" installs it without it doing anything.

firefox.name: Firefox, on any OS
firefox.caveat: Firefox keeps its own certificate store and ignores the system one — import this CA separately in Firefox's own settings, or every HTTPS site will still show a certificate error there even after the OS trusts it.

worldMap.title: Traffic world map
worldMap.note: The rotating globe is rendered live by your browser's own GPU (WebGL2) — a different GPU, and a different pipeline, than the CUDA traffic field on the server. Destination points are real GeoIP data; the gateway itself has no real coordinate here (it never phones out to look up its own public IP), so every arc's local end is a schematic anchor, not a claim about where your house is.
worldMap.noWebgl: This browser doesn't support WebGL2, so the globe can't render.
worldMap.empty: No locatable external connections observed yet.
